titleEn: First Deportation to Babylon (597 BCE)
description: After the siege of Jerusalem in 597 BCE about 7,000 people were exiled to Mesopotamia; Wikipedia dates the later deportation to 587 BCE (the existing "Babylonian Exile" row uses 586).
verbatim_quote: around 7,000 individuals were exiled to Mesopotamia

titleEn: Return to Zion under Cyrus (538 BCE)
description: Cyrus the Great ended the exile in 538 BCE, the year after capturing Babylon; exiled Judeans were permitted to return to Judah.
verbatim_quote: Cyrus the Great ended the exile in 538 BCE

titleEn: Jewish Captives Brought to Rome after Pompey (63 BCE)
titleHe: שבויים יהודים לרומא לאחר כיבוש פומפיוס (63 לפנה"ס)
description: After Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BCE, freed Jewish slaves settled permanently in Rome on the right bank of the Tiber as traders.
verbatim_quote: freed Jewish slaves settled permanently in Rome on the right bank of the Tiber as traders

titleEn: Deportation from Judea to Carthage after the Great Revolt (70-73)
titleHe: הגליה מיהודה לקרתגו אחרי המרד הגדול (70-73)
description: Josephus reports 97,000 Jewish captives sold into slavery during the Great Revolt (66-73 CE) and 30,000 deported from Judea to Carthage. The figures are Josephus' and are generally treated as uncertain.
verbatim_quote: 30,000 Jews were deported from Judea to Carthage by the Romans

titleEn: Bar Kokhba Revolt Deportations to Cyrenaica (132-136)
titleHe: הגליה לקירנאיקה אחרי מרד בר כוכבא (132-136)
description: Jewish tradition holds that the Romans deported twelve boatloads of Jews to Cyrenaica after the Bar Kokhba revolt; captives were sold into slavery. Tradition only, not a documented count.
verbatim_quote: Jewish tradition holds that the Romans deported twelve boatloads of Jews to Cyrenaica

titleEn: Maimonides' Exile from Cordoba (1148-1168)
description: The Almohads conquered Cordoba in 1148; the family of Maimonides, with many other Jews, chose exile and settled in Fez, Morocco.
verbatim_quote: Maimonides' family, along with many other Jews, chose exile.

titleEn: Maimonides' Exile from Cordoba (1148-1168)
description: Maimonides arrived in Acre on 16 May 1165 with his father and brother.
verbatim_quote: arriving on May 16, 1165

titleEn: Maimonides' Exile from Cordoba (1148-1168)
description: The family settled in Fustat (Old Cairo) by 1168; Maimonides finally settled there between 1168 and 1171.
verbatim_quote: The family settled in Fustat

titleEn: Ashkenazi Migration East to Poland (13th-16th c.)
titleHe: הגירת יהודי אשכנז מזרחה לפולין (המאות ה-13 עד ה-16)
description: Massacres during the Crusades, restrictions in the Holy Roman Empire and Black Death persecutions pushed Ashkenazi Jews eastward; by the 16th century the bulk lived in the Kingdom of Poland. Origin city is representative of the Rhineland. Statute of Kalisz (1264) marks the start.
verbatim_quote: by the 16th century, the bulk of the Ashkenazi Jews had migrated to the Kingdom of Poland

titleEn: Ashkenazi Migration East to Poland (13th-16th c.)
titleHe: הגירת יהודי אשכנז מזרחה לפולין (המאות ה-13 עד ה-16)
description: Massacres during the Crusades, restrictions in the Holy Roman Empire and Black Death persecutions pushed Ashkenazi Jews eastward; by the 16th century the bulk lived in the Kingdom of Poland. Origin city is representative of Bohemia. Statute of Kalisz (1264) marks the start.
verbatim_quote: by the 16th century, the bulk of the Ashkenazi Jews had migrated to the Kingdom of Poland

titleEn: Ashkenazi Migration East to Poland (13th-16th c.)
titleHe: הגירת יהודי אשכנז מזרחה לפולין (המאות ה-13 עד ה-16)
description: Massacres during the Crusades, restrictions in the Holy Roman Empire and Black Death persecutions pushed Ashkenazi Jews eastward; by the 16th century the bulk lived in the Kingdom of Poland. Origin city is representative of Austria. Statute of Kalisz (1264) marks the start.
verbatim_quote: by the 16th century, the bulk of the Ashkenazi Jews had migrated to the Kingdom of Poland

titleEn: Sephardic Exile 1492 to Portugal
description: After the Alhambra Decree most of the Spanish exiles migrated to Portugal, which gave only a few years of respite before 1496-97. Origin point is representative of Castile.
verbatim_quote: A majority of Sephardim migrated to Portugal

titleEn: Sephardic Exile 1492 to the Ottoman Empire
description: Sultan Bayezid II welcomed the exiles, mainly to Thessaloniki and Izmir. First arrivals in Salonika in 1492 came from Mallorca and Catalonia; Castile and Sicily followed in 1493.
verbatim_quote: The first arrivals came in 1492 from Mallorca and Catalonia

titleEn: Sephardic Exile 1492 to the Ottoman Empire
description: Bayezid II sent ships to bring Jews to Ottoman ports, mainly Thessaloniki and Izmir. Origin point (Valencia) is representative.
verbatim_quote: Sultan Bayezid II sent ships to bring them, mainly to Thessaloniki and Izmir

titleEn: Sephardic Exile 1492 to Italy
description: Some 9,000 Jews had made their way to Italy in 1492, mainly to the Kingdom of Naples, the Duchy of Ferrara and the Papal States.
verbatim_quote: Some 9,000 Jews had already made their way to Italy in 1492

titleEn: Sephardic Exile 1492 to Italy
description: Duchy of Ferrara was among the main Italian destinations of the 1492 exiles.
verbatim_quote: mainly to the Kingdom of Naples, the Duchy of Ferrara, and the Papal States

titleEn: Portuguese Conversos Emigrate to Amsterdam
description: Conversos leaving Portugal rejoined Jewish communities in Amsterdam, London or Livorno; Sephardim began settling in the Netherlands in the late 16th century after the 1579 Union of Utrecht guaranteed freedom of conscience. Years approximate.
verbatim_quote: Sephardic Jews started to settle in the Netherlands, especially Amsterdam

titleEn: Livornina: Conversos Invited to Livorno (1591-1593)
description: Grand Duke Ferdinando I de Medici issued charters in 1591 and 1593 granting foreign settlers including Jews broad rights; Portuguese and Spanish Marranos found refuge there. Origin point is representative of the Iberian Peninsula.
verbatim_quote: to assure all foreigners desiring to settle at Livorno, including Jews, of the most extensive rights

titleEn: Sephardic Settlement in Dutch Recife (1636-1654)
description: Kahal Zur Israel, the first synagogue in the Americas, was established in Recife in 1636; about 1,450 Sephardic Jews lived there under Dutch rule.
verbatim_quote: Kahal Zur Israel Synagogue was the first synagogue in the Americas, established in Recife in 1636

titleEn: Flight from Recife to New Amsterdam (1654)
description: After the Portuguese retook Recife in 1654, 23 Jews escaped to the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam.
verbatim_quote: 23 Jews from the community escaped to the Dutch North American colony of New Amsterdam

titleEn: Jewish Refugees from Lithuania to Amsterdam (1650s)
description: A large influx of Jewish refugees from Lithuania in the 1650s strained Amsterdam poor relief; the article links the wider migration to the violence of 1648 and after. Origin city representative.
verbatim_quote: A large influx of Jewish refugees from Lithuania during the 1650s

titleEn: Jewish Emigration from the Russian Empire to Britain (1881-1914)
description: Two million Jews fled the Russian Empire between 1880 and 1920, many going to the UK and US; the Aliens Act 1905 introduced immigration controls aimed at reducing the influx of Eastern European Jews.
verbatim_quote: Two million Jews fled the Russian Empire between 1880 and 1920, with many going to the United Kingdom

titleEn: First Aliyah (1882-1903)
description: Between 1881 and 1903 an estimated 25,000-60,000 immigrants, mostly from the Russian Empire and Romania, came to Ottoman Palestine and founded Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Yaakov, Petah Tikva and others in 1882. Odessa as port of embarkation is a representative origin, not stated in the source.
verbatim_quote: The First Aliyah laid the cornerstone for Jewish settlement in Israel

titleEn: Second Aliyah (1904-1914)
description: About 35,000 Jews, mostly from Russia, immigrated into Ottoman Palestine between 1904 and 1914.
verbatim_quote: approximately 35,000 Jews

titleEn: Baron de Hirsch Colonies and Jewish Immigration to Argentina
titleHe: מושבות הברון הירש וההגירה היהודית לארגנטינה
description: The Jewish Colonization Association, founded 1891 by Baron de Hirsch, settled Jews in agricultural colonies in Entre Rios and Santa Fe (e.g. Moises Ville); about 13,000 Jews arrived yearly in 1906-1912 and over 150,000 lived in Argentina by 1920.
verbatim_quote: Roughly 13,000 Jews arrived each year between 1906 and 1912

titleEn: Lithuanian Jewish Immigration to South Africa (1880-1914)
description: South Africa's Jewish population grew from about 4,000 in 1880 to over 40,000 by 1914, accelerating with the 1886 gold rush; so many came from Lithuania that the community was called a colony of Lithuania.
verbatim_quote: So many of them came from Lithuania that some referred to the population as a colony of Lithuania

titleEn: Jewish Immigration to Canada (1881-1914)
description: Pogroms in Russia from the 1880s drove emigration from the Pale of Settlement; by 1914 Canada had about 100,000 Jews, three-quarters in Montreal or Toronto. Origin city representative.
verbatim_quote: By 1914, there were about 100,000 Jews in Canada

titleEn: German Jews to Palestine under the Haavara Agreement (1933-1939)
description: The Haavara Agreement of 25 August 1933 made possible the migration of approximately 60,000 German Jews to Palestine between 1933 and 1939.
verbatim_quote: approximately 60,000 German Jews to Palestine between 1933 and 1939

titleEn: German-Jewish Emigration to the United States (1933-1941)
description: The US accepted roughly 190,000 European Jewish refugees in 1933-43, more than any other country; about 27,000 visas were available in late 1938 against over 300,000 applicants by June 1939.
verbatim_quote: accepting roughly 190,000

titleEn: German-Jewish Emigration to Britain (1933-1941)
description: England accepted about 65,000 Jewish refugees in 1933-43 (all European origins).
verbatim_quote: England accepted about 65,000

titleEn: Jewish Refugees to Shanghai (1938-1941)
description: Shanghai required no visa; estimated arrivals 1,374 in 1938, 12,089 in 1939, 1,988 in 1940 and 4,000 in 1941. About 18,000 were relocated to the Hongkew Designated Area in 1943.

titleEn: Jewish Refugees to Bolivia (1938-1941)
description: Bolivia allowed up to 30,000 refugees to immigrate in 1938-1941; the figure is a permitted quota, not a count of arrivals.
verbatim_quote: allowed for 30000 refugees to immigrate

titleEn: Sosua Refugee Settlement, Dominican Republic
description: After the 1938 Evian Conference the Dominican Republic accepted refugees; the Joint-funded Dominican Republic Settlement Association supported an agricultural settlement for about 700 refugees at Sosua. Years of arrival are not stated in the source.
verbatim_quote: Sosua became a Jewish refugee settlement founded by Jews fleeing the rising Nazi regime of the 1930s

titleEn: Kindertransport (1938-1939)
description: Children from Germany, Austria, occupied Czechoslovakia and Danzig travelled by train to the Netherlands; nearly 10,000 were taken in by the UK.
verbatim_quote: The United Kingdom took in nearly 10,000 children

titleEn: Kindertransport (1938-1939)
description: Austrian children joined the transports to the Hook of Holland.
verbatim_quote: Germany, Austria, occupied Czechoslovakia and the Free City of Danzig

titleEn: Kindertransport (1938-1939)
description: Most transports went by ferry from the Hook of Holland to Harwich; the first party of 196 children arrived on TSS Prague on 2 December 1938.
verbatim_quote: from the Hook of Holland to Harwich

titleEn: Deportation of the Warsaw Ghetto to Treblinka (1942)
description: About 265,000 Jews were transported by freight train from the Warsaw Ghetto to Treblinka between 22 July and 12 September 1942.
verbatim_quote: 265,000 Jews were transported in freight trains from the Warsaw Ghetto to Treblinka

titleEn: Deportation of Hungarian Jews to Auschwitz (1944)
description: Between 15 May and 9 July 1944 over 434,000 Jews were deported on 147 trains, mostly to Auschwitz. Budapest is a representative node; most deportees came from the provinces.
verbatim_quote: Between 15 May and 9 July 1944, over 434,000 Jews were deported on 147 trains

titleEn: Deportation of Salonika Jews to Auschwitz (1943)
description: Deportations began 15 March 1943; a total of 48,974 Greek Jews, most from Salonika, were eventually sent to Auschwitz, finishing early August.
verbatim_quote: A total of 48,974 Greek Jews, most from Salonika, would eventually be sent to the camp

titleEn: Brihah: Survivors Move from Poland to the West (1944-1948)
description: Brihah moved approximately 250,000 survivors from Poland, Romania, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia into Austria, Germany and Italy (article flagged for sparse citations).
verbatim_quote: Bricha transferred approximately 250,000 survivors

titleEn: Brihah: Survivors Move from Poland to the West (1944-1948)
description: Route to the Displaced Persons camps in Germany.
verbatim_quote: moving survivors into Austria, Germany, and Italy

titleEn: Brihah: Survivors Move from Poland to the West (1944-1948)
description: Route onward to Italy.
verbatim_quote: moving survivors into Austria, Germany, and Italy

titleEn: Sh'erit Hapleta: Displaced Persons to Israel (1945-1952)
description: By 1952 most Jewish displaced persons had left the camps: about 136,000 settled in Israel, roughly 80,000 in the United States, about 20,000 elsewhere. Origin (Munich) represents DP camps in Germany, Austria and Italy.
verbatim_quote: About 136,000 settled in Israel

titleEn: Sh'erit Hapleta: Displaced Persons to the United States (1945-1952)
description: Roughly 80,000 Jewish displaced persons settled in the United States by 1952.
verbatim_quote: roughly 80,000 in the United States

titleEn: Aliyah Bet: Illegal Immigration from Romania (1934-1942)
titleHe: עלייה ב': עלייה בלתי לגאלית מרומניה (1934-1942)
description: Over 100,000 people attempted illegal entry to Mandatory Palestine (142 voyages, 120 ships); ships sailed from Constanta and Sulina in Romania. Year range is the Nazi-era phase named in the source.
verbatim_quote: Over 100,000 people attempted to illegally enter Mandatory Palestine

titleEn: Aliyah Bet: Interned in Cyprus (1945-1948)
description: Most intercepted immigrants were sent to British internment camps in Cyprus, which held as many as 50,000 people. Years follow the post-war phase named in the source.
verbatim_quote: internment camps in Cyprus

titleEn: Exodus 1947: Sete to Haifa
description: The ship left Sete on 11 July 1947 with 4,515 refugees and was intercepted off Palestine on 18 July.
verbatim_quote: 4,515 refugees

titleEn: Exodus 1947: Haifa to Port-de-Bouc
description: Passengers were moved to three ships that left Haifa on 19 July and reached Port-de-Bouc on 2 August; they refused to disembark voluntarily.
verbatim_quote: reached Port-de-Bouc near Marseille on August 2

titleEn: Exodus 1947: Port-de-Bouc to Hamburg
description: The ships reached Hamburg on 7 September 1947, where passengers were disembarked.
verbatim_quote: the migrants were successfully disembarked

titleEn: Operation Magic Carpet: Yemen to Israel (1948-1950)
description: Between 16 December 1948 and 24 September 1950 Israel took in approximately 49,000 Yemenite Jews, flying from Aden.
verbatim_quote: between 16 December 1948 and 24 September 1950 to take in approximately 49,000 Yemenite Jews

titleEn: Operation Ezra and Nehemiah: Iraq to Israel (1951-1952)
description: Between 120,000 and 130,000 Iraqi Jews were airlifted to Israel; Iraq's March 1950 law permitted emigration on condition of renouncing citizenship; about 6,000 remained.
verbatim_quote: airlifted between 120,000 and 130,000 Iraqi Jews to Israel via Iran and Cyprus from 1951 to 1952

titleEn: Operation Yachin: Morocco to Israel (1961-1964)
description: After the 1961 Egoz sinking more than 70,000 Moroccan Jews left over three years, mainly through Operation Yachin (HIAS financed about $50 million). Destination shown is Israel; some went elsewhere.
verbatim_quote: more than 70,000 Moroccan Jews left the country

titleEn: Jewish Exodus from Algeria to France (1961-1962)
description: Between late 1961 and late summer 1962, 130,000 of Algeria's approximately 140,000 Jews left for France.
verbatim_quote: 130,000 of Algeria's approximately 140,000 Jews left for France

titleEn: Jewish Exodus from Libya to Israel (1948-1951)
description: Over 30,000 Jews emigrated from Libya to Israel between 1948 and Libyan independence in December 1951.
verbatim_quote: Over 30,000 Jews emigrated to Israel between 1948 and Libyan independence

titleEn: Evacuation of Libyan Jews to Italy (1967)
description: In 1967 the government evacuated over 4,000 Libyan Jews to Italy; 1,300 later went to Israel and 2,200 remained in Italy.
verbatim_quote: over 4,000 Libyan Jews

titleEn: Jewish Emigration from Iran to Israel (1948-1978)
description: David Littman puts the total of emigrants to Israel in 1948-1978 at 70,000; about one-third of Iranian Jews, mostly poor, emigrated to Israel in 1948-1953 (Sanasarian estimate).
verbatim_quote: the total figure of emigrants to Israel in 1948-1978 at 70,000

titleEn: Soviet and Post-Soviet Jewish Aliyah to Israel (1971-2000)
titleHe: עלייה מברית המועצות ומחבר העמים לישראל (1971-2000)
description: Soviet exit visas rose in the 1970s (245,951 Jews received visas 1971-1980; destinations not broken down in the source); emigration surged from 1989 and 1,037,000 ex-Soviet Jews lived in Israel by 1999 (Wikipedia infobox).

titleEn: Post-Soviet Jewish Emigration to the United States (1989-2000)
titleHe: הגירת יהודים מבריה"מ לשעבר לארצות הברית (1989-2000)
description: In the late 1980s and early 1990s more than half of the Soviet Jewish population left, most for the US, Israel, Germany, Canada and Australia; about 350,000 ex-Soviet Jews lived in the US by 2004.
verbatim_quote: more than half of the population leaving, most for the United States, Israel, Germany, Canada and Australia

titleEn: Post-Soviet Jewish Emigration to Germany (1989-2000)
description: Germany is among the main destinations of post-Soviet Jewish emigration; 178,500 ex-Soviet Jews lived there in 2011 (infobox).
verbatim_quote: Germany 178,500 (all ex-Soviet, 2011)

titleEn: Operation Moses: Ethiopian Jews from Sudan to Israel (1984-1985)
titleHe: מבצע משה: יהודי אתיופיה מסודן לישראל (1984-1985)
description: From 21 November 1984 to 5 January 1985 some 8,000 Ethiopian Jews were flown from Sudan via Belgium to Israel.
verbatim_quote: some 8,000 Ethiopian Jews

titleEn: Operation Solomon: Gondar to Addis Ababa (1991)
description: Jews from Gondar province were brought to Addis Ababa by bus and truck before the airlift.
verbatim_quote: brought to Addis Ababa by bus and truck

titleEn: Operation Solomon: Addis Ababa to Israel (1991)
description: On 24-25 May 1991, 35 aircraft transported 14,325 Ethiopian Jews to Israel.
verbatim_quote: 35 aircraft transported 14,325 Ethiopian Jews to Israel
